blocks.text: Leaving a job, retiring, or consolidating retirement accounts can create more decisions than it seems. Should you leave your 401(k) where it is? Roll it into an IRA? Move it to a new employer plan? Convert some or all of it to Roth?

At PointOak, we help you evaluate each option in the context of your complete financial picture. We consider taxes, investment choices, future income needs, Social Security, Medicare, and your long-term retirement goals before recommending a strategy.

sections.title: Why Rollover and Roth Conversion Planning Matters

blocks.text: A rollover and a Roth conversion are not the same thing, but the decisions often overlap.

A rollover changes where your retirement assets are held. A Roth conversion changes how those assets are taxed. Either choice can affect your future income, taxes, investment flexibility, and retirement strategy for years.

The right answer depends on more than your current tax bracket or account balance. It should also account for your age, retirement timeline, employer-plan features, future required distributions, Social Security, Medicare, and the rest of your financial life.
That is why we evaluate these decisions together rather than treating them as isolated transactions.
If your employer retirement plan holds company stock, don't automatically sell or roll the position without first understanding the potential consequences.
Certain distributions of employer securities from a qualified retirement plan can involve specialized tax considerations, including potential net unrealized appreciation (NUA) treatment.
Whether that strategy is available or appropriate depends on the specific circumstances.
PointOak can help identify when employer stock warrants additional analysis and coordinate with your tax professional before implementing a rollover or distribution.

body.text: Retirement assets generally move directly from the employer plan to the receiving retirement account.
Assets are distributed to the participant first, which can introduce withholding requirements, deadlines, and other tax considerations.
Whenever possible, we help clients understand the mechanics before initiating the transaction, so the movement of assets is coordinated with the intended financial strategy.

items.title: Evaluate All of Your Rollover Options

body.text: Leaving an employer does not automatically mean you should roll your 401(k) into an IRA.
We help you compare the options available to you, including leaving assets in your former employer's plan, moving them to a new employer plan, rolling them into an IRA, or taking a distribution.
Roth conversion planning often works best as a multi-year strategy.
We help evaluate how much to convert and when based on your current and projected income, retirement timeline, future required distributions, and broader financial plan.
A Roth conversion can increase taxable income in the year of conversion and may affect other areas of your retirement plan.

We consider how conversion income may interact with tax brackets, Social Security taxation, Medicare-related income thresholds, and your other income sources while coordinating with your tax professional as appropriate.
Your employer-sponsored plan may offer benefits or investment options worth preserving.
We compare fees, investment choices, account protections, distribution rules, and other plan-specific considerations before recommending a rollover.

items.title: Integrate the Decision With Retirement Income

body.text: Rollover decisions affect more than where your money is invested.
We consider how each account may eventually be used for retirement income, how withdrawals fit together, and how the decision supports your broader retirement strategy.

items.title: Avoid Decisions You Cannot Easily Reverse

body.text: Roth conversions are generally permanent once completed.
Our role is to help you understand the potential consequences before moving forward so the strategy fits both your current circumstances and long-term goals.

a.text: A 401(k) rollover moves retirement assets from one qualified retirement account to another.
Depending on your circumstances, that may mean moving an old 401(k) into an IRA or transferring it into a new employer-sponsored retirement plan.

items.q: Should I roll over my old 401(k)?

a.text: Your options generally include leaving the account in your former employer's plan, rolling it into an IRA, transferring it to a new employer plan if permitted, or taking a distribution.
Each option comes with different considerations around taxes, fees, investment choices, access to funds, and account protections. We evaluate those differences before recommending a rollover.

items.q: What is the difference between a 401(k) rollover and a Roth conversion?

a.text: A rollover changes where your retirement assets are held. A Roth conversion changes their tax treatment.

A direct rollover from a traditional 401(k) to a traditional IRA generally maintains tax-deferred status. A Roth conversion moves pre-tax assets into a Roth account and generally creates taxable income in the year of conversion.

items.q: Can a Roth conversion affect Medicare premiums?

a.text: A Roth conversion increases taxable income in the year it occurs, which may affect Medicare income-related premium adjustments in later years.
We consider those potential effects when evaluating the size and timing of a conversion.

items.q: Can a Roth conversion affect how much of my Social Security is taxable?

a.text: Conversion income can increase your overall taxable income, which may affect how much of your Social Security benefits are included in taxable income.
That is one reason we evaluate Roth conversions alongside Social Security and broader retirement income planning rather than in isolation.

items.q: Can I undo a Roth conversion?

a.text: Roth conversions can no longer be recharacterized back to a traditional IRA under current rules, so it's important to evaluate the strategy carefully before completing the conversion.

items.q: What should I consider before rolling over a 401(k)?

items: Investment choices.
Plan fees.
Account protections.
Access to funds.
Your retirement timeline.
Tax consequences.
Whether your new employer accepts rollovers.
How the account fits into your broader retirement income plan.
Your employer plan may offer advantages that an IRA does not, so a rollover should never be treated as automatic.
